title: What is mocking and stubbing: mock is a fake object that tracks how it was called (verify interactions), stub is a fake that returns preset values (control behavior): and what tools are used (Mockito, WireMock)?
shortTitle: What is mocking and stubbing, and the tools used

s1_definition.oneliner: A stub returns preset values to control what the code sees, a mock also records calls so you can verify interactions, and you create them with Mockito for Java objects and WireMock for HTTP services.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Stub** – A fake that returns preset values to control what the code under test sees. Used for state-based assertions.
- **Mock** – A fake that records how it was called so you can verify interactions: method, arguments, call count.
- **Mockito** – Standard Java library for creating test doubles of classes and interfaces.
- **WireMock** – Fake HTTP server for mocking external REST APIs with configurable responses, delays, and faults.
- **Other doubles** – Dummies (passed but unused), fakes (lightweight implementations), spies (wrap real objects).
- **Right boundary** – Mock external or slow collaborators, not the class under test. Do not over-mock.
s1_definition.analogy: When testing the National Bank of India's transfer logic in isolation, you do not want to hit the real fraud-check service or the real email sender, because they are slow, external, and unpredictable. So you use fakes. A stub is a stand-in that simply gives a canned answer, for example a fake fraud service that always says "approved," so you can control what the transfer logic sees. A mock is a stand-in that also keeps a log of how it was used, for example a fake notification service that records "you called me once with Rajesh's email," so you can verify that the transfer logic actually tried to notify the customer. Tools like Mockito create these fakes for Java objects, and WireMock creates a fake HTTP server for external web services.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Mocking and stubbing are ways to replace a real dependency with a fake, a test double, so I can test a unit in isolation, fast, deterministic, and free of external systems. The distinction is intent. A stub is about controlling behavior: I configure it to return preset values or throw specific exceptions, so I control the conditions the code under test experiences, and then I assert on the state or output the code produces. For example I stub a rate service to return a fixed exchange rate so I can assert the converted amount, without caring how many times it was called. A mock is about verifying interaction: it records how it was called, and after exercising the code I verify that the expected calls happened, the right method, the right arguments, the right number of times. I use a mock when the correct behavior is the interaction itself, for example verifying that a successful transfer calls the notification service exactly once and a blocked transfer does not call it at all. In short, stubbing answers does my code produce the right output given this input from the dependency, and mocking answers did my code interact with its collaborators correctly.

The tools make this practical. Mockito is the standard Java library for creating doubles of classes and interfaces, where I stub methods with thenReturn or thenThrow and verify interactions with verify and times or never, plus argument matchers and captors. WireMock addresses the HTTP boundary, standing up a fake HTTP server I program to return specific responses, status codes, bodies, headers, delays, and faults, so I can test code that calls an external REST API deterministically, including error and slow responses.

The nuances I stress are to mock at the right boundary, the external or slow collaborators, not the class under test, and not to over-mock, because verifying too many interactions couples tests to implementation detail and makes refactoring painful, so I stub for state-based assertions and mock only when the interaction genuinely is the behavior worth asserting. I also keep the real thing in higher-level contract or integration tests, because mocks verify my code against my assumptions, which could be wrong. At the National Bank of India I stubbed the fraud service to drive both the allowed and blocked branches of the transfer logic, mocked the notifier to verify a successful transfer notified the customer exactly once and a blocked one never did, and used WireMock to simulate the exchange-rate API including a timeout so I could test how the code handled it. Being able to define stub versus mock precisely, control behavior versus verify interaction, and name Mockito and WireMock with how I use each is what shows an interviewer I write isolated, deterministic tests the right way.

Remember one sentence: a stub controls what the code sees by returning preset values, a mock verifies how the code interacts by recording calls, and you choose based on whether you assert state or interaction.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Test Doubles: Stub vs Mock
  ───────────────────────────

  STUB (control behavior)         MOCK (verify interaction)
  ┌──────────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────────┐
  │ Returns preset values │       │ Records calls made   │
  │                       │       │                       │
  │ rateService.getRate() │       │ notifier.send(email) │
  │   -> returns 74.5     │       │   -> recorded!       │
  │                       │       │                       │
  │ You assert: the       │       │ You verify: send was │
  │ converted amount is   │       │ called once with     │
  │ correct               │       │ rajesh@bank.in       │
  └──────────────────────┘       └──────────────────────┘

  Tools:
  Mockito -> Java objects (both stub and mock)
  WireMock -> HTTP services (fake server)
```

keyPoints: A stub returns preset values to control what the code under test sees, used for state-based assertions
A mock records how it was called so you can verify interactions: method, arguments, call count, order
Mockito creates test doubles for Java objects: mock, stub methods, inject, verify interactions
WireMock creates a fake HTTP server for external REST APIs with configurable responses, delays, and faults
Mock at the right boundary: mock external or slow collaborators, not the class under test
Prefer stubs for state-based assertions and mocks only when the interaction itself is the behavior to verify
